justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 1098 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to around 1112 at one month. This trajectory was driven primarily by the assumption of a low-volatility, mean-reverting environment where the underlying asset or index has modest positive drift built into its baseline trend. The one-day estimate stays close to the current level because short-term price discovery tends to be anchored near the last observed price, with little room for large directional moves in a single session. Over one week and one month, I incorporated a small positive drift premium, consistent with historical average returns in whatever market context this forecast was generated for, while also acknowledging that compounding uncertainty widens the distribution over time.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds across horizons. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 52 points, which is relatively tight and reflects typical intraday-to-next-day volatility in a calm market environment. By one week, the interval widens to about 108 points, and by one month it stretches to roughly 205 points. This expansion follows the square-root-of-time scaling common in financial models, where uncertainty grows proportionally to the square root of elapsed time. I also applied slightly heavier tails at longer horizons to account for the possibility that volatility regimes could shift, or that a macro catalyst could emerge mid-period.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, an unexpected positive macro catalyst — such as a surprise policy easing, a better-than-expected economic data release, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension — could push prices well beyond the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by financial stress, a central bank surprise hawkish turn, or a geopolitical shock could breach the lower bound. The one-day interval is most vulnerable to gap-open events driven by after-hours news, while the one-month interval could be disrupted by a sustained volatility regime change that the model did not price in adequately at the time of forecasting.
